pageData.title: The Aymara Kingdoms
pageData.titleline: The Aymara Kingdoms - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Aymara Kingdoms. The Aymara kingdoms - also called the lake kingdoms - developed between 1150 and 1477 CE in the high plateau around Lake Titicaca, in the region Andeans called Qullaw, after the disappearance of Tiwanaku left a political vacuum. In its wake, a number of Aymara-speaking, independent, and rival kingdoms emerged, among them the Lupaca, the Colla, the Pacajes, and the Azangaros. Their world was divided between Urcosuyu - 'male, fire' - on the western side of the lake and Umasuyu - 'female, water' - on the eastern side, and their societies often had two leaders apiece; most of these kingdoms buried their leaders in tower-shaped mausoleums, and each held lands at different altitudes in what scholars call a 'vertical archipelago'. These kingdoms matter because they kept the Andean altiplano's ancient ways alive through the centuries between empires, and their lords would play decisive roles in the fate of the Inca.
pageData.para2: The kingdoms warred constantly - above all the rivalry between the Aymara kurakas of Chucuito, of the Lupaca kingdom, and Hatunqulla, of the Colla kingdom. When the Inca pressed south, the Lupaca leader Cari faced the Colla leader Chuqui Capac, who attacked the Lupacas near Paucarcolla before the Inca army arrived; after a long battle near Hatunqulla, Chuqui Capac was taken prisoner, and the Colla lands were subdued - some by force, others peacefully. Destroyed towns were repopulated with mitmakunas, resettled colonists, and the Aymara kingdoms accepted the dominion of Cuzco while keeping their lands and their far-off colonies in the eastern mountains. That arrangement survived until the first years of the Spanish conquest, when the kingdoms' territorial and political dismemberment began.

pageData.title: The Chimú Empire
pageData.titleline: The Chimú Empire - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Chimu Empire. The Chimu were the largest and most prosperous culture of the Late Intermediate Period along the Peruvian coast, flourishing between the 12th and 15th centuries CE with their capital at the great city of Chan Chan. The Chimu constructed cities and developed large-scale irrigation systems using canals, and there seems to have been much social stratification. Rulers like Guacricaur expanded into the Moche, Santa, and Zana valleys, and in 1375 CE, under Nancinpinco, the Chimu conquered the Lambayeque (Sican) culture, absorbing some of its cultural practices; tribute extracted through successful military campaigns and political coercion made them the dominant regional power, with Chan Chan the capital of administrative centers across the valleys. This empire matters because it was the last great coastal civilization before the Inca, and its methods - in administration, craft, and imperial organization - were studied by its conquerors.
pageData.para2: The Chimu spoke the Yunca language - also called Mochica or Moche - now extinct and definitely distinct from the Inca tongue, and they produced characteristic black ware ceramics. Their imperial system was sophisticated: conquered rulers were allowed a certain autonomy, and compounds of foreign artisans were gathered in the capital, a policy the Inca would later adopt. The empire's independence ended when the Inca, under Pachacuti Inca Yupanqui and his son Topa Inca Yupanqui, conquered it between 1465 and 1470 CE, capturing the 11th known Chimu ruler, Minchancaman, around 1470; thereafter the Chimu became a vassal state within the Inca Empire. Yet the story does not end there - the imperial playbook the Inca inherited, from road-fed tribute to artisan compounds, carried the imprint of the coastal kingdom it had absorbed.

pageData.title: The Inca Empire (Tahuantinsuyu)
pageData.titleline: The Inca Empire (Tahuantinsuyu) - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Inca Empire: Tahuantinsuyu. The Inca Empire, known to its people as Tahuantinsuyu - 'The Four Parts Together' - arose sometime in the early 1400s and became the largest indigenous empire of the Americas. How much of that growth owes to a single great leader, an Alexander-the-Great-like Pachacuti? Scholars note the Incas had been developing the capability for conquest over four to six generations, though the 1586 chronicle of the Spanish cleric Miguel Cabello Valboa dates Pachacuti's reign to 1438-1471 and his son Tupac Inca Yupanqui's to the years that followed. The empire matters because it bound the Andes into a single administered world, from imperial Cuzco outward, through a system of administration and infrastructure unmatched anywhere in the pre-Columbian Americas.
pageData.para2: At the heart of that system was a vast network of roads - some 40,000 kilometers according to John Hyslop, the leading scholar of the subject - built to move armies and administrative resources across a hugely varied landscape, connecting the capital to provincial centers, with many smaller branches extending to outposts east and west; the roads varied in width and style because Inca leaders often utilized existing routes. Around Cuzco, workers received their food from state storehouses every four days or even daily, and below the emperor, religious officials and magistrates called kurakas oversaw the day-to-day administration of their regions, collecting taxes, overseeing day-to-day administration, and even choosing brides for the men of their communities. The empire's end came swiftly: after a devastating civil war between the half-brothers Atahualpa and Huascar, the Spaniard Pizarro captured and executed Atahualpa, dealing a fatal blow to what had been the largest indigenous empire of the Americas.

pageData.title: The Muisca Confederation
pageData.titleline: The Muisca Confederation - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Muisca Confederation. The Muisca civilization flourished in the fertile eastern highlands of what is now Colombia between 600 and 1600 CE, its territory encompassing modern Bogota and its environs, and it has gained lasting fame as the origin of the legend of El Dorado - 'The Gilded One'. A Muisca ceremony held at Lake Guatavita - actually only one of many kinds - involved a ruler being covered in gold dust; the Spanish, hearing this story, allowed their imagination and lust for gold to leap beyond the bounds of reality, and soon a legend arose of a magnificent golden kingdom. This confederation matters because its goldwork is among the great artistic traditions of the Americas: for the Muisca, gold was not used as a currency but as an artistic medium, mined from exposed veins and panned from mountain rivers.
pageData.para2: The Muisca goldsmiths employed a wide range of techniques - lost-wax casting, a two-tone finish, repousse, soldering, granulation, and filigree - and hammered gold into thin sheets on round stone anvils. Their tunjos - small votive figures of snakes and flat male, female, and animal forms in gold alloy - were placed at sacred sites, and elite members of society wore pectorals, earrings, and nose studs. Nor did they restrict their art to gold: they created fine textiles of wool or cotton. There is ample evidence that commodities such as gold, shells, feathers, animal skins, tobacco, salt, and coca leaves moved through Muisca markets in a thriving regional trade. When the Spanish arrived in the 1530s, drawn by the very legend the Muisca had inspired, this rich highland world was drawn into the colonial age.

pageData.title: The Chachapoya Culture
pageData.titleline: The Chachapoya Culture - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Chachapoya, called the Warriors of the Clouds by the Inca, built some of the most spectacular cities in the Americas on misty mountaintops in northern Peru. Their homeland lay in the cloud forests of the eastern Andes, where ridges rise above the Utcubamba River valley and rain feeds dense forests draped in orchids and bromeliads. From about 800 CE, Chachapoya communities constructed settlements of circular stone houses decorated with geometric friezes in zigzag and diamond patterns, a style found nowhere else in the Andes.
pageData.para2: The greatest Chachapoya monument is Kuélap, a walled fortress-city perched on a limestone ridge at three thousand meters. Its outer wall rises up to twenty meters high and stretches for hundreds of meters, pierced by only three narrow entrance passages that funnel into steep ramps, easy to defend. Inside, more than four hundred circular buildings housed a population of several thousand. Kuélap was once thought to be purely a fortress, but archaeologists now see it as a political and ceremonial center for the surrounding region, occupied for centuries and remodeled many times.
pageData.para3: Chachapoya society was organized in local chiefdoms rather than a single kingdom, and the cloud forest peoples farmed terraced fields of maize, potatoes, and beans, raised llamas, and traded with the coast and the Amazon lowlands. They buried their dead in spectacular fashion, placing mummies in chullpas, small burial houses built into cliff faces, and in the famous sarcophagi of Karajía, two-meter-tall clay figures perched on a cliff ledge that once held mummy bundles. Spanish chroniclers later described the Chachapoya as tall and fair-skinned, giving rise to fanciful legends of lost European tribes, but archaeology shows they were a local Andean people.
pageData.para4: In the 1470s the Inca emperor Topa Inca Yupanqui conquered the Chachapoya after hard fighting, deporting many thousands under the Inca resettlement system. When the Spanish arrived decades later, some Chachapoya allied with them against the Inca, and the region became a base for early Spanish expeditions toward the Amazon. Kuélap, once known as the Machu Picchu of the north, is now a major archaeological park reached by cable car, and ongoing excavations continue to reveal the sophistication of this cloud-forest civilization.

pageData.title: The Tairona and the Sierra Nevada Chiefdoms
pageData.titleline: The Tairona and the Sierra Nevada Chiefdoms - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Tairona civilization flourished on the Caribbean slopes of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta in Colombia, building stone cities on jungle ridges and crafting some of the finest goldwork of the ancient Americas. From the early centuries CE, Tairona communities terraced the steep mountainsides of the world's highest coastal mountain range, creating a network of stone-paved paths, plazas, stairways, and circular house platforms. At its height around 1000-1500 CE, the Tairona population may have numbered in the hundreds of thousands across the Sierra Nevada's northern slopes.
pageData.para2: The most famous Tairona site is Ciudad Perdida, the Lost City, known to the local Kogi people as Teyuna. Built from about 800 CE, it consists of over two hundred stone terraces linked by stairways, crowning a ridge deep in the forest. It was rediscovered by looters in the 1970s, sparking a treasure rush before the government secured the site. Other major centers included Pueblito and Bonda. Tairona towns were connected by stone roads that ran along the ridgelines, parts of which still survive and are used by Indigenous communities today.
pageData.para3: Tairona artisans were master goldsmiths, working in the lost-wax technique to cast intricate pendants of bat-men, jaguars, and shamans in tumbaga, a gold-copper alloy. Their ceramics included incised blackware jars, and they carved stone batons, beads, and ceremonial seats. Tairona religion centered on the Sierra Nevada itself, regarded as the heart of the world, with priests maintaining cosmic balance through ritual. This worldview survives strikingly intact among the Kogi, Arhuaco, Wiwa, and Kankuamo peoples, the Tairona's direct descendants, who still farm the same terraces and walk the same stone paths.
pageData.para4: Spanish contact brought catastrophe. Coastal Tairona towns were drawn into the pearl and slave trades, and from the 1520s Spanish expeditions pushed inland, meeting stiff resistance. After decades of war, the surviving Tairona withdrew into the high Sierra, where their descendants preserved their traditions in isolation for centuries. Today the Kogi and their neighbors are recognized as guardians of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, and Ciudad Perdida, reached by a multi-day jungle trek, has become one of South America's great archaeological destinations.
pageData.source4label: Journal of Field Archaeology: Tairona settlement research

pageData.title: The Mapuche before the Conquest
pageData.titleline: The Mapuche before the Conquest - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Mapuche, the people of the land, developed in the valleys and forests of south-central Chile into one of the most resilient Indigenous societies of the Americas. Their ancestors had inhabited the region for thousands of years, and by about 600 CE their communities were settling into farming life, cultivating maize, potatoes, quinoa, and beans and raising llamas. The Mapuche never formed a centralized state. Instead they lived in scattered, largely autonomous communities organized around extended families, each led by a lonko, or headman, with religious life guided by shamans called machi, usually women.
pageData.para2: Mapuche society was decentralized but far from primitive. Communities gathered for collective labor, feasts, games, and councils where disputes were settled and war leaders chosen. Their world stretched from the Itata River south toward Chiloé, encompassing coastal ranges, fertile central valleys, and the northern edges of the rainy southern forests. They traded with peoples of the Andes and the Argentine pampas, adopting technologies and ideas while fiercely guarding local independence. Silver work later became a Mapuche hallmark, with elaborate jewelry worn by women of status.
pageData.para3: The first empire to test Mapuche independence was the Inca. In the late fifteenth century, Inca armies pushed south through Chile, incorporating the northern valleys as far as the Maule River. At the Maule they met the Mapuche and their allies, and after a major battle, commonly placed around the 1470s-1480s, the Inca advance stopped. The Maule became a frontier: north of it lay the Inca province of Chile, south of it the unconquered Araucanía. The Mapuche learned from the encounter, adopting some Inca military and political ideas while rejecting Inca rule.
pageData.para4: When the Spanish arrived in the 1540s, they found no emperor to capture, only hundreds of determined communities. The Mapuche destroyed the first Spanish towns in the south and in 1553, under the toqui Lautaro, defeated and killed the conquistador Pedro de Valdivia. Thus began the Arauco War, which would burn for three centuries, the longest resistance in the Americas. The Mapuche remained independent in their heartland until the 1880s, and today they are the largest Indigenous people of Chile, still defending land and language.
pageData.source3label: Country Studies (Library of Congress): Chile: The Indigenous Population

pageData.title: The Diaguita of the Southern Andes
pageData.titleline: The Diaguita of the Southern Andes - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Diaguita. In the dry valleys that cut between the Andes of northwestern Argentina and northern Chile, the Diaguita built one of the most distinctive cultures of the pre-Columbian south. From around AD 900 they terraced the steep valley sides, drew irrigation canals from the snowmelt rivers, and raised maize, beans and quinoa in one of the driest inhabited regions on earth. Their villages of stone and adobe climbed the hillsides; their largest, the Quilmes citadel of the Calchaqui valleys, held several thousand people within its rings of walls and terraced fields.
pageData.para2: The Diaguita were master potters: their funerary urns, painted in black, white and red with geometric designs and stylized faces, are among the finest ceramics of ancient South America. They worked copper and bronze, herded llama, and their chiefs ruled valley confederations linked by kinship and trade across the cordillera. Their society was organized and warlike, and their hilltop strongholds - pucaras - commanded every approach to the valleys.
pageData.para3: Around 1470 the expanding Inca Empire came down the valleys and, after hard fighting, absorbed the Diaguita lands. The conquerors deported whole communities - the empire's device of resettlement - and imposed their own officials and gods, yet Diaguita identity endured under the new order. When the Spaniards arrived a lifetime later, it was the Diaguita who met them with the longest and fiercest resistance in the south: the Calchaqui Wars, above all the great rising of the 1630s and the long guerrilla of the chief Pedro Chamijo, held the valleys against Spain for over a century.
pageData.para4: The last Diaguita resistance was broken in the 1660s, and defeat and deportation scattered the people - many were carried as far as the environs of Buenos Aires. The valleys' identity, though, never died: the Diaguita are today a recognized indigenous people of Argentina and Chile, and the ruins of Quilmes, rising against the Calchaqui hills, remain the monument of a nation that fought two empires in turn.

pageData.title: The Kingdom of Quito
pageData.titleline: The Kingdom of Quito - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Kingdom of Quito. High in the northern Andes, on the plateau where the equator crosses the mountains, the city of Quito was old before the Incas came. The people the Spanish chroniclers called the Quitu had farmed the valley from the first millennium, and by about the eleventh century their chiefs had joined with the migrating Cara people - conquerors or allies from the coast, the traditions differ - to form the realm remembered as the Kingdom of Quito, or the Kingdom of the Caras, with its lords styled shyri.
pageData.para2: The shyris ruled from their ceremonial center at Caranqui and, later, from Quito itself, over a valley grown rich on maize and the trade of the mountain corridor. Their realm was no empire but a confederation of chiefdoms - Cayambe, Otavalo, Puruha, Canari to the south - whose lords acknowledged, married into, or fought the shyri's house as advantage turned. The kingdom's astronomers watched the sun from the equator line itself, and the monument at Cochasqui, with its pyramids and its alignment of ramps, still marks where they measured the passing year.
pageData.para3: The kingdom's fate was bound to the Inca advance. From the late fifteenth century the armies of Tupac Yupanqui and then Huayna Capac pressed north past the Canari and into the plateau; the northern peoples resisted in a long and bitter war, remembered in Ecuadorian tradition as the struggle of the Caras against the invaders, before Quito itself fell around the turn of the century. Huayna Capac made the conquered city his own - he rebuilt it as an Inca administrative capital, mothered his heir Atahualpa with a Quitu princess, and ruled the northern empire from it.
pageData.para4: When civil war split the Inca world, Atahualpa held Quito against his brother in Cusco, and it was the northern, Quitu-based army that won him the empire - months before Pizarro's landing destroyed them both. The conquistadors found Quito already burned by its own defenders, and refounded it in 1534 on the ashes of the shyris' city. The Kingdom of Quito left no chronicles of its own, but its name still carries the memory of a sovereign Andean realm before the Inca.

pageData.title: The Guarani Peoples
pageData.titleline: The Guarani Peoples - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Guarani. In the centuries before Europeans came, the forests and grasslands of what is now Paraguay, southern Brazil, northeastern Argentina and Uruguay were home to the Guarani, a family of peoples speaking dialects of one language and sharing one way of life. Their own traditions remember a long migration: the search for yvy mara e'y, the Land Without Evil, a paradise beyond the sea or the forest, that drove their chiefs and prophets to lead whole communities on journeys of hundreds of miles across the rivers and forests of the southern continent.
pageData.para2: The Guarani lived in large communal villages of longhouses, each housing an extended family under its chief, set in clearings in the forest. They were shifting cultivators, growing maize, manioc, sweet potatoes and beans in gardens cleared by fire, and hunters and fishers of the great rivers. War and the prestige of captives ran through their world - the chroniclers dwelt, with fascinated horror, on their war rituals - but so did a rich mythology of the hero twins and a poetry of prophecy that shaped their migrations and their resistance.
pageData.para3: When the Spaniards reached Paraguay in the 1530s, the Guarani became their providers, allies and wives; the mestizo society of the River Plate grew from that meeting, and the Guarani language entered the blood of Paraguay itself. In the seventeenth century the Jesuits gathered tens of thousands of Guarani into the famous reductions - the missions of Paraguay - which sheltered them from the slave-raiders of Sao Paulo and created a unique communal Christian republic, until the missions were destroyed and their people scattered after 1767.
pageData.para4: The Guarani outlasted missions, wars and the terrible Paraguayan War, and their language achieved what no other native tongue in the Americas has: today Guarani is an official language of Paraguay, spoken by mestizo and Indian alike - the living proof that the people of the Land Without Evil endure.
pageData.source2label: UNESCO: Jesuit Missions of the Guaranis

pageData.title: The Tupinamba of the Brazilian Coast
pageData.titleline: The Tupinamba of the Brazilian Coast - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Tupinamba. When the Portuguese first sailed down the coast of Brazil around 1500, the people who watched them from the beaches were the Tupinamba, the most numerous and formidable nation of the coastal forests, kin to the Guarani and speakers of a Tupi language. From the Amazon's mouth to Sao Vicente their villages of palm-thatched longhouses commanded the shores that Portugal would claim: warlike, skilled canoe-men, farmers of manioc, and the makers of the red featherwork capes that became the first treasures of Brazil in the cabinets of Europe.
pageData.para2: Tupinamba society turned on the vendetta between villages and the fate of war captives. Prisoners might live for years among their captors, married and honored, before the great communal ritual of execution and the feast that followed - the practice that so appalled and fascinated the first Europeans that the name of the Tupinamba became a byword for cannibalism in sixteenth-century Europe. Yet the same coast produced the century's most extraordinary eyewitness accounts: the German gunner Hans Staden, held captive among them, and the French Calvinist Jean de Lery, whose memoir of living in a Tupinamba village is a founding text of anthropology.
pageData.para3: The first decades of contact were a bewildering traffic: French traders from Honfleur and Huguenot settlers of Antarctic France at Rio allied with the Tupinamba against the Portuguese, and the Tupinamba fought on both sides of the European quarrel, masters of their coast for sixty years. Mem de Sa's destruction of the French at Rio in 1567 and the smallpox that followed broke their power; disease, slavery and war then consumed the coastal villages within a century.
pageData.para4: The Tupinamba of the coast vanished as a nation, absorbed into missions and plantations or driven into the interior, where related Tupi peoples survived. Their language lived on as the lingua geral, the lingua franca of colonial Brazil, spoken by Portuguese and mameluco for two centuries, and their words - for the animals, plants and foods of Brazil - entered Portuguese itself: jaguar, tapioca, piranha, toucan.

pageData.title: The Peoples of Patagonia
pageData.titleline: The Peoples of Patagonia - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Peoples of Patagonia. At the cold bottom of the inhabited world, where the Andes drown in the channels of Tierra del Fuego and the steppe runs a thousand miles to the Atlantic, human beings made a home at the uttermost edge. The peoples of Patagonia were among the last on earth to be reached by outsiders, and among the most wrongly remembered: the tall Tehuelche hunters of the steppe, whom Magellan's sailors called Patagones - big-feet - and Europe turned into giants; the Yamana and Selk'nam of the Fuegian channels, who went nearly naked in the sub-Antarctic wind and kept fires in their canoes; the Kawesqar, nomads of the fjords.
pageData.para2: Each people had solved an impossible environment. The Tehuelche of the open steppe lived by the guanaco and the rhea, hunting with the boleadora, the three-stoned throwing weapon of the plains, and following the herds in great seasonal gatherings where marriages were made and the dead remembered. The canoe peoples of the channels - Yamana, Kawesqar, Chono - lived from the sea entirely: shellfish, sea lions, beached whales, their bark and later plank canoes carrying whole families through waters where no land life was possible. The Selk'nam of northern Tierra del Fuego hunted the guanaco and staged the Hain, the great initiation ceremony in which the young men confronted the painted spirits of the spirits' lodge.
pageData.para3: Their prehistory was ancient - the coastal middens and the cave paintings of the Rio Pinturas, the Cave of the Hands, were thousands of years old when Europeans came - and their contact with Europeans came late and disastrously: the sheep ranches that fenced the Tehuelche's hunting grounds in the 1880s, the gold rush and the bounty-hunting of the Selk'nam in Tierra del Fuego, and the epidemics that followed every contact. Within two generations of the Conquest of the Desert and the sheep, the nations of Patagonia were broken.
pageData.para4: Yet the ending was not the story. For at least ten thousand years the peoples of Patagonia had thrived where almost no one else could live, and their descendants - Tehuelche, Yamana, Kawesqar, Selk'nam - survive to reclaim their names and histories today. The Cave of the Hands is a World Heritage Site, and the giant Patagons of Magellan's chronicler have given way to the memory of the most southerly nations of mankind.
pageData.source2label: UNESCO: Cueva de las Manos, Rio Pinturas
